cards.text: Psalm 149 kicks off with "Hallelujah!" The psalmist calls God's people to sing to the LORD a new song, and this one is NOT a solo. A NEW song, friend, not the same three songs you've had on repeat in the car since forever.

cards.question: The psalmist wants God's people singing this new song together. Where does he want God's praise sung?

answers.text: In the assembly of the godly
On the shore of the Jordan

cards.text: Next, Israel is called to rejoice in their Maker, the One who made them. In the same breath, the psalmist calls Him their King.

cards.question: The psalmist calls God Israel's Maker and their King. Who does he call to rejoice in their King?

cards.text: Then the psalmist gets specific about HOW God's people should praise. He doesn't leave it up to guesswork, friend. He spells it out.

cards.question: How does the psalmist want God's people to praise His name?

cards.text: Dancing, tambourine AND harp. I can't play either one, friend, and my only dance move is hopping on this gold base. HOP. That's the whole routine.
Then the psalmist gives the reason behind all this joy.

cards.question: True or false: the psalmist says the LORD takes pleasure in His people.
The LORD dresses some people up in salvation. He adorns the ___ with salvation.

cards.text: Next the saints are called to exult in glory. And the psalmist has a spot picked out for the shouting.

cards.question: Where does the psalmist say the saints should shout for joy?

cards.text: Most of us lie in bed going over the bills. These saints lie there shouting for JOY, and then the psalm turns serious.

cards.question: With God's high praises in their mouths, the saints hold a ___ in their hands.
True or false: the psalmist pictures the saints' sword being used to inflict vengeance on the nations.
The psalmist pictures the nations' nobles in shackles of iron. Who else does he picture bound with chains?

cards.text: All of this is to execute the judgment written against them. Then the psalmist calls it an honor.

cards.question: The psalmist calls carrying out the judgment written against the nations an honor. Who does he say this honor is for?
Psalm 149 opened with "Hallelujah!" True or false: it closes with that same word.

findings.problem: The setup gives the answer away. Card 1 says the new song 'is NOT a solo', and the question adds 'singing this new song together'. Only 'In the assembly of the godly' is a gathering of people, and the wrong answers are geographic places. So the right answer stands out as a different kind of thing.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The right answer is a group setting (an assembly of people), while both wrong answers are geographic locations ('In the fields of Bethlehem', 'On the shore of the Jordan'). The answers are not the same kind of thing, so the right one stands out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank asks the baker to supply the exact word of the line 'He adorns the afflicted with salvation.' Card 8 only says a reason is coming, so nothing lets the baker reason out 'afflicted' over 'mighty' or 'wealthy'. This tests wording the baker hasn't seen, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Asking where the saints shout for joy ('Upon their beds') is a pure detail guess. Card 11 only says 'the psalmist has a spot picked out', which gives no basis to reason it out. This matches the Psalm 23 'guessing a detail' bad example and does not ask about movement or meaning.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The card says 'These saints lie there shouting for JOY' as if it is happening. Psalm 149:5 is a call: 'let them shout for joy upon their beds.' The card should keep it as the psalmist's call.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The question says 'the saints hold a ___ in their hands' as a fact. Psalm 149:6 is a wish: 'May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands.' The question should keep the 'may' framing.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The card asks about the repeat of 'Hallelujah!' at the close of the psalm. Card 1 already told its first appearance. The repeated line should be asked about only where it first appears, not on its return.

rule.text: When a line repeats, like a psalm's refrain, ask about it only the first time it appears.

findings.problem: Most story cards are flat narration with little of Papa Dorin's voice: cards 3, 8, 11 and 17 have no humor, and card 5 is mild. Only cards 1, 7 and 13 have real jokes. The stop reads more like a nice dad being pleasant than laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
